source: Wikipedia (read 2026-11) Conceptual blending, section on integration network types (citing Birdsell 2014; Fauconnier & Turner 2003)
finding: Gives the four network types. Simplex: one input holds an organizing frame, the other holds specific values; the frame roles are filled with those values in the blend. Mirror: all spaces share the same organizing frame. Single-scope: inputs have different frames, but only one frame organizes the blend. Double-scope: inputs have different frames and the blend takes parts of both.
numbers: No empirical numbers. Lists vital relations (cause-effect, change, space, identity, role, part-whole) and cites the Buddhist-monk riddle as the mirror example.
limits: Secondary source. The page gave no worked example for simplex, single-scope or double-scope, so those definitions rest on the summary, not on the primary text.
agent_relevance: The type is defined by one question: how many organizing frames reach the blend (0 new, 1, or 2). That is a checkable label the agent can assign to a plan.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks, Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187
finding: Founding paper: a four-space model (two inputs, generic space, blend) with selective projection, plus a list of optimality principles (integration, topology, web, unpacking, good reason, metonymic tightening). Network types are developed in the 2002 book and in Turner's 1998 chapter 'Figure'.
numbers: None: the paper analyses hand-picked examples and reports no experiment.
limits: The markturner.org web copy returned only a stub (title page, 560 characters) and the Wiley PDF returned 403, so the full text was NOT read. Content here is from secondary sources that I did open (Coulson & Oakley 2000; Wikipedia; Turner's 2026 draft).
agent_relevance: The theory is a procedure description, not a tested mechanism. Treat it as a design vocabulary.

source: Coulson & Oakley (2000) Blending basics, Cognitive Linguistics 11(3/4):175-196
finding: Primer on blending by its main experimental advocate. States the six optimality constraints: integration, topology, web, unpacking, good reason, metonymic tightening. Says satisfying them is selective and they often conflict, so the best-fitting reading is the likely one.
numbers: No numbers. A primer.
limits: Constraints are guidelines, not tested rules. Covers the four-space model but gives little on the simplex, mirror, single-scope, double-scope typology.
quote: satisfaction of these principles is selective, and satisfying one constraint is often inconsistent with satisfying another
agent_relevance: If the agent scores candidate blends, the constraints can be a rubric (does the blend run as one unit; does it keep the input relations; can you unpack it) but they trade off, so use code-side checks, not a single score.

source: Coulson & Oakley (2000) Blending basics - on the testability critique
finding: Records the critique (Gibbs 2000) that blending theory is too powerful, explains everything and so nothing, and works by post hoc analysis of chosen examples. Authors accept that analysis must move past post hoc work but defend ad hocness as a feature of an interpretive model.
numbers: None.
limits: A defence by theory insiders. No independent test of whether network type predicts anything is given.
quote: we agree that blending analyses must move beyond post hoc analysis
agent_relevance: No human study shows that choosing a network type improves reasoning. Any use in the agent is a design bet [D], not an evidence-backed step.

source: Coulson & Oakley (2000) Blending basics - computational models (Veale & O'Donoghue 2000, Sapper)
finding: Reports that Veale & O'Donoghue (2000) built Sapper, a computational blending model shaped by the optimality principles. It explains the felt novelty of metaphors, extension of metaphors, and revival of dormant ones, and shows the principles can be implemented algorithmically.
numbers: No evaluation numbers given in the review.
limits: Reported secondhand. Sapper is a spreading-activation model over a hand-built semantic net; it was shown tractable, not shown to match human judgements.
agent_relevance: Earlier computational route: explicit graph search with constraint scoring. It maps to code-selected candidate blends (guardrail G5), unlike a free LLM judgement.

source: Coulson & Oakley (2000) Blending basics - neural account (Grady 2000)
finding: Reports Grady's (2000) proposal that spreading activation could implement 'completion': imagining a philosopher debating Kant may activate a debate frame. Also notes Grady's account of selective projection as binding and inhibition, and flags that projection is often described as if people build full inputs and then choose among them.
numbers: None.
limits: A proposal with no data in this review. Selective projection is the least constrained step of the theory.
agent_relevance: Completion (pulling in an unstated frame) is where an LLM is strongest and least reliable. Anything it completes should be checked against the inputs.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study, Memory & Cognition 30(6):958-968
finding: ERP test of the blending claim that literal and figurative meaning use the same integration process. Eighteen adults read sentences ending in a word used literally, as a literal mapping (a literal use that forces mapping, e.g. 'used cough syrup as an intoxicant'), or metaphorically. N400 (300-500 ms) was smallest for literal, largest for metaphor, intermediate for literal mapping.
numbers: N=18. N400 main effect of sentence type F(2,34)=3.90, p<.05. Metaphor vs literal F(1,17)=6.86, p<.02. Linear trend across the three types F(1,17)=6.86, p<.02, quadratic F<1; the linear trend accounted for over 98% of sentence-type variance. A 'binary cut' contrast (literal=literal mapping) explained only about 40%. Literal mapping did not differ reliably from either neighbour (F=2.03, F=2.18).
limits: Single study, 18 readers, 279 sentences. Cloze probability and associative priming are possible confounds (the authors checked weak associates: 15 of 279 sentences). Tests graded integration cost, not network types. Metaphor also gave a larger late posterior positivity; literal mapping gave an unexpected frontal positivity (replication needed, authors say).
quote: Literal endings elicited the smallest N400, metaphors the largest N400, whereas literal mappings elicited an N400 of intermediate amplitude.
agent_relevance: Supports a gradient view: the more mapping between domains a step needs, the higher the integration cost. For the agent, treat cross-frame steps as costlier and more error-prone than same-frame steps.

source: Coulson & Matlock (2001) Metaphor and the space structuring model, Metaphor & Symbol 16(3/4):295-316
finding: Off-line feature-listing study: people listed features of a word alone or at the end of a literal, literal-mapping, or metaphoric sentence. Feature sets shifted most from the bare word for metaphoric contexts, least for literal, with literal mapping between. Emergent features appeared in all three, which the authors read as completion and elaboration working across the literal-figurative range.
numbers: Cosine similarity of feature sets to the null-context set: 0.84 (literal), 0.81 (literal mapping), 0.78 (metaphoric). Context effect F(2,68)=5.48, p<.01; literal vs metaphorical t(1,34)=3.26, p<.01; literal mapping differed from neither. 35 stimuli, 20 raters per word in null context, 10 per word per sentence condition.
limits: Small differences in similarity (0.78 to 0.84). Features were coded off-line, so it does not show online blending or any specific network type. Cosine measure was computed on a semantic-space vector model.
agent_relevance: Gives a measured example of emergent structure: context changes what features of a concept are used. Emergence can be tested by comparing the feature set with and without the second frame.

source: Gibbs (2000) Making good psychology out of blending theory, Cognitive Linguistics 11:347-358 (and Gibbs 2001 reply in same journal), as reported by Wikipedia and Coulson & Oakley 2000
finding: Main psychological critique: blending lacks testable hypotheses, is a framework not one theory, and infers processes from products (finished expressions). Other theories may explain the same cases.
numbers: None. Known only as summarised in two opened sources (a01 Wikipedia, a04).
limits: I did not open the Gibbs paper (paywalled; the DOI is the Crossref record found for 'Making good psychology out of blending theory', 2001 issue date). Year given inconsistently across sources (2000 vs 2001).
agent_relevance: Same as a04: the typology should be treated as untested for reasoning gains.

source: Ritchie (2004) Metaphor and Symbol 19 (blending critique), as reported by Wikipedia
finding: Argues the minimal network needs at least four spaces, but many blends can be explained by simpler integration processes, and the Buddhist monk example has an alternative reading.
numbers: None.
limits: Known only through the Wikipedia summary (opened); the original paper was not read. Fauconnier (2021) reply was only named, not read.
agent_relevance: Warns that a four-space network may be more machinery than needed for simple combination; a simplex or single-scope step may be just a function call with slots.

source: Turner (2026) blending page, markturner.org/blending.html, items on the 2026 CogSci and ACL conferences
finding: Turner's own index lists current work: a 2026 CogSci draft on formal conceptual blending, an ACL 2026 poster 'Evaluating Creative Generative AI with Conceptual Blending' (Xi, Cheng, Soni, Turner), the Kombine benchmark (2509.21043), and Sato 2025 (2505.10948). It reproduces the Buddhist-monk riddle as the standard teaching blend.
numbers: None on the page itself.
limits: Index page. The ACL 2026 poster PDF failed to download as a valid PDF, so its results were not read.
agent_relevance: Shows where current AI work on blending sits: benchmarks (Kombine), a position paper (formal blending) and prompt-level probes (Sato). No result yet shows a network-type scaffold lifting task accuracy.

source: Gomez-Ramirez & Turner (2026 working draft) Formal conceptual blending as a fundamental tool for artificial mathematical intelligence and for the fine-tuning of LLMs
finding: Position paper. States that integration networks come in several named types (refers to Turner 1998 'Figure'), restates metaphor as an asymmetrical, compressive kind of blend, formalises blending as a pushout in category theory, and proposes blending-aware fine-tuning losses and benchmarks for maths reasoning traces.
numbers: No measured results. A text search for accuracy figures found none; it only proposes losses and benchmark design.
limits: Working draft dated 2026-07-24, not peer reviewed. The proposal is not tested. It describes the monk riddle's generic space: a monk traversing the path from one end to the other from dawn to sunset, without direction, position or day.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete, if untested, recipe: keep the blend's provenance and an unpacking path back to both inputs so a step can be audited. This fits G2/G3 (revise from real output; check on held-out facts).

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring Combinatorial Creativity in Large Language Models and Humans (Kombine), arXiv 2509.21043v6
finding: Large benchmark with association, analogy and blending tasks over random entity pairs. LLMs are 10-16 points better at association and analogy than blending; the bottleneck is finding a shared abstraction (generic space), not building the blended space.
numbers: 35 LLMs, temperature 0.9. Valid outputs averaged over models: association 59.0%, analogy 53.4%, blend 43.4%. Given a valid generic space, models built a coherent blend 97.1% of the time. Best blender scored 64.8% (vs 55.4% on analogy for same model, as stated in the paper). Task correlations: analogy-blending r=0.70, association-blending r=0.54.
limits: Judges are LLM panels (three models); judge agrees with human judgement 75% of the time when the panel is unanimous. Entities are random Wikidata pairs, not tasks from a reasoning benchmark. Model names are as printed in the paper.
agent_relevance: For our agent the weak step is abstraction: finding what two frames share. A code check that the proposed generic space holds for BOTH inputs is the highest-value gate before any blend is built.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Kombine - operational definition of single-scope, double-scope and double-scope emergent
finding: Turns the typology into a 0-3 integration-quality score Q: 1 if both inputs project structure (single-scope in their wording), 2 if the projected structures also intersect on a shared property (double-scope), 3 if the blend also has emergent structure true of neither input (double-scope emergent). Cites Fauconnier & Turner (2008).
numbers: Q in {1,2,3}. Utility, surprise and originality scored alongside. Shared prompt requires at least one 'uv' triple (a property both inputs organize) and one emergent triple.
limits: This is a loose rendering. In Fauconnier & Turner single-scope means ONE organizing frame is projected and the other only supplies content; Kombine counts it as 'both inputs contribute'. So Kombine's scale is a new metric, not a test of the 2002 typology.
agent_relevance: A ready scoring recipe for a blend: shared slot present (double-scope) and an emergent claim that can be checked. Usable as a code-side rubric.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Kombine - human comparison
finding: 75 Prolific adults did the same tasks. Humans scored below every LLM tested on each task, and both groups found blending hardest.
numbers: Humans vs LLM (mean): association 22.1% vs 59.0%; analogy 32.9% vs 53.4%; blending 12.8% vs 43.4%. 120 recruited, 75 kept after screening for AI use; five items per task.
limits: Humans skipped items scored zero; the gap is driven mainly by utility (finding a valid connection), per the authors. Non-expert online sample.
agent_relevance: Blending is hard even for strong models. Do not assume the model can pick double-scope on request; require a visible shared slot.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Kombine - inventive homogeneity
finding: Models invent near-identical concepts. One in five invented concepts reuses a property another model invented. Models reuse other models' properties 14 times more often on blends than on analogies, and same-provider models do so 2.3 times more than cross-provider.
numbers: 2,070 invented concepts, 7,868 properties; similarity threshold 0.674 (99th percentile of property-pair cosine). Rates as stated in the abstract.
limits: Homogeneity measured by embedding similarity of properties; threshold is a chosen percentile.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrail G4: samples from related models are not independent. A 'double-scope' blend from the same model repeated N times will often be the same blend.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma & Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with LLMs, CHI '23 (arXiv 2111.04920)
finding: GPT-3 finds connecting concepts between a pop-culture domain and a product (a task close to building a blend's shared slot). Three strategies (no GPT, half GPT, full GPT) were equally accurate, and humans using the tool produced more blend ideas than with a search baseline.
numbers: 56.7% of connecting concepts related to both domains overall (no-GPT 56.0%, half-GPT 55.3%, full-GPT 58.7%). At least one good result among five: 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3% (93.3% of all pairs). GPT-3 attribute accuracy by type: adjectives 79%, activities 58%, catchphrases 35%; overall 57%. Scene relatedness: product scenes 89.1%, pop-culture scenes 75.9%. User study: 10 participants, 2.03 (SD 0.84) blend ideas per pair with tool vs 0.87 (SD 0.56) baseline, Wilcoxon p<0.001; mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80, p=0.004.
limits: Small within-subject study (10 people, 6 pop-culture-product pairs). About half of suggestions wrong, so a person still filters. Measures idea counts, not quality or correctness of the blends. Does not use network-type labels.
agent_relevance: An LLM proposes shared concepts with roughly 57% precision per item but one good option among five about 93% of the time. Generate several, filter with code or a check, pick one.

source: Ge & Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models, arXiv 2106.14127
finding: Language models find a relevant second object and a shared property for a given object (e.g. moon sliced like an orange), then an image model draws it. LMs beat a ConceptNet knowledge base on a simile dataset; CLIP-based generators beat DF-GAN in human preference. Questions were built from the optimality principles (unpacking, integration).
numbers: Precision on the simile set at P@1000 reached 37.33 for BERT-large, 53.08 for a GPT model and 66.38 for the best row (table columns are garbled in the extracted text, so the model label for each row is uncertain). 20 blend descriptions, six questions, each answered by 9 Mechanical Turk subjects; BigSleep and DeepDaze significantly above DF-GAN at 95%, BigSleep above DeepDaze.
limits: Old models (BERT, GPT-2 class, CLIP-guided BigGAN). Tests visual blending only, and the human rating is preference, not correctness. Table row labels not recoverable from the text I extracted.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that LMs find the shared property well. The unpacking and integration principles can be turned into rating questions, which an agent can mimic as checks.

source: Olearo, Longari, Raganato, Penaloza & Melzi (2025) Blending concepts with text-to-image diffusion models, arXiv 2506.23630
finding: Four zero-shot blending methods in diffusion models (embedding averaging, prompt switching, alternating prompts, split U-Net conditioning) compared on 22 concept pairs. No method wins everywhere. Three of the four are order-sensitive: swapping which concept is the 'main' one changes the image, much like a single-scope blend with a dominant frame.
numbers: 100 participants ranked all four methods on 22 pairs. ALTERNATE preferred over SWITCH in 51% of comparisons (not significant). Only the embedding-average method is order-symmetric.
limits: Images, not text reasoning. Authors say seed variation also changes results and the sample was lay participants. Map to frame asymmetry is my reading, not the authors' claim.
agent_relevance: Which input is the 'main' frame changes the result. For a text agent, run both orderings and keep the one a check accepts.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs, arXiv 2505.10948
finding: Review and position paper mapping blending onto prompts: input spaces are concepts in the prompt, the generic space is pretraining knowledge, the blend is the output. Defines Prompt-Induced Transition (shift of tone from a blended prompt) and Prompt-Induced Hallucination (plausible but unfounded output from blending distant domains, e.g. the periodic table with tarot).
numbers: No measurements in the paper text I read.
limits: No experiment, sample, or metric reported. The neural parallels (engram integration in mice, language cortex) are suggestive, not tested. Blending distant domains is shown as a source of hallucination.
agent_relevance: A warning: blending far-apart frames can yield fluent output with no ground. Gate any blend on a check against facts before using it.

source: Lu, Leung, Swearngin, Nichols & Barik (2025) Misty: UI prototyping through interactive conceptual blending, CHI '25 (arXiv 2409.13900)
finding: An LLM tool where a developer blends chosen parts of an example UI into work-in-progress code, with a semantic diff to accept or reject each change. Developers could use it, but imperfect blends needed tweaking.
numbers: Frontend developers did 103 blending operations; mean satisfaction after each operation 3.2 of 5 (median 3, SD 1.3). Global blending was used 36 times of 103.
limits: Small formative study with working frontend engineers, no control condition in the part I read. Satisfaction is self-report. Uses blending as an interaction idea, not the network-type taxonomy.
agent_relevance: Showing the change as a reviewable diff, with each part accepted separately, matches the 'revise only from real output' pattern.

source: Cappa, Lippolis & Zoia (2025) Meanings are like onions: a layered approach to metaphor processing, arXiv 2507.10354
finding: Proposes a three-layer metaphor representation (context, blending analysis, pragmatics) built on a Blending Ontology that encodes the four-space network (input, generic, blend, mappings). Example: 'every cigarette is a bullet' as a blend of a weapon frame and a smoking frame.
numbers: None: a modelling proposal with a GitHub ontology, no evaluation reported in the text I read.
limits: Formal framework only; no tested LLM result in this paper. Does not distinguish the four network types in what I read.
agent_relevance: A machine-readable schema for a blend (blendables, blending principle, blended) that could store provenance for each step.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (2002) The Way We Think: conceptual blending and the mind's hidden complexities. Basic Books
finding: Book source for the typology and the claim that double-scope networks, with clashing frames and creative emergent structure, are the cognitively modern form. Wikipedia attributes the four-type description to this work.
numbers: None: argued by examples.
limits: Not opened. Statements here are from the opened secondary sources (a01, a03, a12). The page links the book chapters but gives no experiment.
agent_relevance: The claim 'double-scope is for novel ideas' is the theory's own; no study found tests it against single-scope in a reasoning task.

source: Eppe et al. (2018) A computational framework for conceptual blending, Artificial Intelligence 256:105-129
finding: Formal computational account of blending (generalisation, amalgams, an HDTP-style analogy engine, blend ranking) and metrics for optimality principles, demonstrated in maths and music. Described in Turner's page abstract.
numbers: Not read. Turner's page summary says metrics capture 'most of the so-called optimality principles'.
limits: Publisher page returned 403; arXiv lookup found nothing. Summary taken from Turner's list entry only.
agent_relevance: Prior art for code-side ranking of candidate blends.

source: Veale & O'Donoghue (2000) Computation and blending, Cognitive Linguistics 11(3/4):253-281 (as reported in Coulson & Oakley 2000)
finding: Sapper: a computational blending model implementing the optimality constraints and stretching or contracting structure to fit two domains at different granularity (e.g. car pistons/crankshaft vs animal leg muscle).
numbers: None given in the secondary report.
limits: Original not opened. Description comes from a03/a05.
agent_relevance: Granularity mismatch is a real failure in cross-frame mappings: check that matched roles are at the same level.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) - side findings useful for blending claims
finding: Metaphor sentences had a larger late posterior positivity; literal-mapping sentences a distinct frontal positivity, which authors tie to mental-state reasoning (74% of literal-mapping sentences described pretense, lying or mistaken identity).
numbers: 74% of literal-mapping sentences involved pretense/lying/mistaken identity. N=18.
limits: Authors call the frontal effect unexplained and requiring replication. Another study (Pynte et al. 1996) did not find a reliable positivity for metaphors in a cloze-matched comparison.
agent_relevance: Weak: mapping across frames may recruit extra processing beyond simple meaning lookup. No direct use.
